name: Finding the Command Line
brief:
Before you configure anything you have to be able to move around. A Cisco device has modes, and the command you need only works in one of them. Typing a global command at the user prompt does not produce a helpful error, it produces a caret and a shrug.

This lab is pure navigation. Nothing you do here changes how the network behaves.
watchFor: The prompt tells you where you are. `>` is user EXEC, `#` is privileged EXEC, and anything with parentheses is a configuration mode. Read it before you type.

tasks.text: Get from user EXEC into privileged EXEC on R1.
tasks.hint: The command is `enable`. Watch the prompt change from > to #.

tasks.text: Use context-sensitive help: type `show ?` and read what comes back.
tasks.hint: A question mark at any point lists what is legal next. This is the single most useful key on the device.

tasks.text: Run `show version` and find the IOS version.
Run `show ip interface brief` to see every interface at once.
tasks.hint: Abbreviate it: `sh ip int br`. Everything on this device is administratively down right now.
`hostname WCTA-R1` in global configuration mode. The prompt changes immediately.

tasks.text: Enter interface configuration mode for GigabitEthernet0/0, then come back out with `end`.
tasks.hint: `interface g0/0` gets you in. `exit` steps back one level; `end` goes all the way to privileged EXEC.

extension: Find three more commands that work in privileged EXEC but not in user EXEC. Use `?` at each prompt and compare the two lists.
debrief: Two habits pay for themselves all season: abbreviate everything, and press `?` the moment you are unsure. Under a round clock, `sh ip int br` and a question mark are worth more than memorising syntax you half remember.
